SEC23A-01.note: Negative adverb 'Rarely' forces inversion; the subject is plural 'saplings' and the participle 'grown' needs perfect 'have', not 'do'. 'has its' draws on the singular 'summer'/'orchard' and 'do its' on plural agreement without checking the participle.

SEC23A-02.note: Head noun 'coat' takes singular 'shields'; the embryos belong to the seeds, so 'their'. 'shield their' is the attractor from 'seeds'; 'shields its' tempts by matching the pronoun to the verb's subject.

SEC23A-03.note: 'Many a' takes a singular verb, and the present 'appears' fixes present tense, so 'is'. 'are' is attractive because 'many' reads as plural.

SEC23A-04.note: Subject 'twins' is plural; the absolute phrase about the singular 'infant' interrupts; present 'review' sets tense. 'is breathing' takes the bait of 'infant'/'chest'.

SEC23A-05.note: Head 'swabs' is plural; 'when the fungus appeared' sets past, so 'were shipped'. 'was shipped' draws on 'a single laboratory' in the comparison.

SEC23A-06.note: 'Biochar' is the singular subject; the 'or ...' phrase is an appositive gloss, not a second subject; 'until the autumn rains return' sets present. 'are being spread' tempts through 'fragments'.

SEC23A-07.note: 'for' is a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses, so a comma goes before it. The semicolon before a conjunction is only accepted with long, internally punctuated clauses, which this is not; no comma at all invites the garden path 'season for newborn lambs'.

SEC23A-08.note: 'both in X and in Y' is a correlative pair joining two phrases, so no punctuation goes before 'and'. The comma (A) is attractive because the phrases are long; 'and, in' is plainly wrong.

SEC23B-01.note: In the inverted sentence the subject is plural 'seams', which follows the verb; 'came up' fixes past, so 'were'. 'was' is attractive because 'concern' or 'crews' gets read as the subject, and 'is/are' because of the present-tense frame.

SEC23B-02.note: 'All that survives' is singular (cued by 'survives'); 'when the observatory closed' takes simple past, which rules out present perfect. 'were packed' is attractive through 'instruments'/'crates'.

SEC23B-03.note: 'The former' is the single anemometer; habitual present 'whenever a storm brings' gives present, so 'is checked'. 'are checked' tempts through 'pines'/'gauges'.

SEC23B-04.note: Subject 'footsteps' is plural, and the 'not the steady breeze' contrast does not count; 'crossed' sets past. 'was shaking' takes the bait of 'breeze'.

SEC23B-05.note: 'the longest of which' is singular; 'until groundwater broke through' sets past progressive. 'were being lined' tempts through 'tunnels'/'rings'.

SEC23B-06.note: The elliptical comparison stands in for the lexical verb 'hold', so the pro-verb is 'do', agreeing with plural 'terraces'. 'are' is attractive because a 'be' form feels natural after a comparison, and 'does' copies the singular 'holds'.

SEC23B-07.note: 'most broke apart within seconds' is an independent clause, so the semicolon is needed. A is a comma splice that reads like 'most of which'; D's paired commas are garbled.

SEC23B-08.note: A colon after a complete clause introduces the list that names the three minerals. The comma (B) is attractive but blurs the nested list with the outer series; the semicolon is not followed by an independent clause.

SEC23C-01.note: The 'So quickly ... that' inversion puts the auxiliary before singular 'slang'; 'spreading' needs progressive 'is', not 'does'. 'are' tempts through 'leagues'/'schools', and 'does' through the 'So quickly does X spread' pattern.

SEC23C-02.note: 'which' refers to both pieces (as 'side by side' confirms), so it is plural; present 'compare' gives present progressive. 'is being restored' is attractive because it agrees with the nearest noun, 'screen'.

SEC23C-03.note: Head 'hypothesis' is singular, so 'owes', and the plausibility belongs to the hypothesis, so 'its'. 'owe their' tempts through 'scribes', and 'owes their' through a mixed reading.

SEC23C-04.note: 'founder and first director' names one person (the later 'she'/'her' confirm it), so the verb is singular; 'when she suffered' sets past. 'were compiling' is attractive because the subject looks compound.

SEC23C-05.note: In the concessive 'Faded as X are' the subject is plural 'frescoes', and the main clause 'is easy' sets present. 'were' is the strongest distractor (plural but past); 'is' copies the main verb.

SEC23C-06.note: The fronted object 'This last ledger' is not the subject; the subject is 'archivists', and 'when a burst pipe flooded' takes past progressive. 'was transcribing' is attractive because it agrees with the fronted 'ledger'.

SEC23C-07.note: A list inside an appositive is set off with a matched pair of dashes. A's commas blur the list into the sentence; C (no marks) and D (dash/comma mismatch) can be rejected on sight.
SEC23C-07.drop_reason: Matched-dash appositive list where two of three distractors can be rejected on sight and the third is a familiar comma trap; it reads as easy and would not sit among the hardest SEC items on the module-2 hard route.

SEC23C-08.note: With three engravers, 'Vidal' is a restrictive appositive that picks out which one, so it takes no commas. The paired commas (A) are the strong distractor; B and C each have a single unpaired comma and can be rejected by pattern.

tells: Format skew: 16 of 24 items (all of A-01..A-06, B-01..B-06, C-01..C-06) are 2x2 verb grids (singular/plural x past/present, or a do/have/be auxiliary). Once the format is learned, the test-taker needs only two binary decisions, and the tense half is always settled by one other finite verb in a 'when/while/until/whenever' clause (A-04 'review', A-05 'appeared', A-06 'return', B-01 'came up', B-04 'crossed', B-05 'broke', C-02 'compare', C-04 'suffered', C-06 'flooded'). A test-taker can scan for that clause's tense without parsing the main clause.

Partial attractor tell: in most agreement items the noun right before the blank disagrees in number with the key (A-02 seeds, A-04 infant, A-05 laboratory, B-02 instruments, B-03 pines, B-04 breeze, B-05 tunnels in the relative clause, C-02 screen, C-06 archivists vs fronted ledger). The heuristic 'choose the number opposite to the nearest noun' would win often, though not always (A-03, A-06, C-03, C-04 break it).
Punctuation items: an option with a mismatched or single unpaired mark always loses (C-07 D, C-08 B/C, B-07 D, A-08 D). Key letters are balanced at 6/6/6/6, so there is no letter tell.
near_duplicates: fronted phrase forcing inversion with the subject after the verb
verb number crossed with possessive pronoun in a 2x2 grid
passive progressive 'being' grid with a singular/plural attractor
simple past passive with a misleading noun inside the subject phrase
plural subject interrupted by a phrase about a singular noun, progressive tense
past progressive anchored by a 'when' clause
choosing the clause-boundary mark between two independent clauses

phase2_note: All 24 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses) and every explanation produces its key and accounts for each distractor. Only C-07 is dropped, on difficulty. Batch-level concerns, not per-item drops: 18 of 24 items share the 2x2 number-by-tense verb grid, with tense set by a single 'when/while/until' clause. Near-duplicate pairs should not share a form: A-01/B-01/C-01 (inversion), A-02/C-03 (verb plus pronoun), A-06/B-05/C-02 (passive progressive). Note on A-07: Coherent; its claim that a semicolon before a coordinating conjunction is never conventional overstates the rule (Chicago allows it between long clauses that have their own commas), but the conclusion holds for these short clauses.
